name: Garveyism
scope: The doctrine of Marcus Garvey and the Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA) in the 1910s-1920s: race-first Black nationalism and Pan-Africanism, Black economic self-reliance and a redeemed Africa for the Africans of the world, together with the UNIA's own civil religion (its ritual, Catechism and Chaplain-General) that Burkett's scholarship treats as part of Garveyism. Defining texts: Garvey's Philosophy and Opinions (ed. Amy Jacques Garvey) and the 1920 Declaration of Rights of the Negro Peoples of the World. Excluded: later movements that drew on Garvey (Rastafari, the Nation of Islam, Nkrumah-era Pan-Africanism) and the UNIA's later splinters.

summary: Garveyism is the race-first Black nationalism and Pan-Africanism of Marcus Garvey and the Universal Negro Improvement Association. Its Declaration of Rights (1920) claims all Negroes as citizens of Africa and demands "Africa for the Africans at home and abroad", self-determination for all peoples, control of Africa's wealth and an end to segregation and lynching. Garvey held that races should keep their racial purity and that a race needs its own industry and government, and he founded politics on belief in God.
